entries.title: Philippa Walton
entries.description: Businesswoman, mother and pioneering owner of the Waltham Abbey gunpowder mills, whose family became closely connected with Mickleham.

entries.transcription:
In grateful Memory
of
(the best of Wives, Mothers, and Friends)
Mrs PHILLIPA WALTON
Daughter and Coheiress
of
JOHN BOURCHIER M.D.
and
Relict of WILLIAM WALTON
late of LONDON Merchant,
(A Gentleman worthy of and happy, in
her tenderest Affection.)
His early Death left Her a Young & mournfull Widow.
Charged with the Care of Ten helpless Infants:
Of Whom Six Sons and Three Daughters survived,
to Comfort the Life and lament the Death of their
Excellent and Amiable Parent;
Who, after having secured and improved their Property
by her Application & Address, and formed their
Minds by her Instructions & Example,
retired from the Hurry of Active Life,
to end her Days in Piety & Peace.
She died
(in Calm & Christian Serenity)
on the 7th day of December 1749,
in the 74th Year of her Age,
and is Interred near this Place.

story.standfirst: A pioneering businesswoman whose remarkable life connects the Waltham Abbey gunpowder industry with St Michael & All Angels, Mickleham.
story.caption: Philippa Walton’s memorial inside St Michael & All Angels. Parish/archive photograph supplied for this project.

sections.title: A remarkable woman remembered at Mickleham

paragraphs.text: Inside St Michael & All Angels, an elaborate eighteenth-century monument invites us to remember Philippa Walton. Its words begin with family and friendship. Beyond them lies the story of a woman who carried responsibility for a household and a substantial industrial business.

Philippa’s story belongs to two places: the mills at Waltham Abbey and the church at Mickleham, where her son became Rector. The surviving memorial brings that wider history into the space visitors can still enter today.

Born Philippa Bourchier around 1674, she married William Walton, a London merchant. The monument names her as the daughter and co-heiress of John Bourchier M.D. It remembers ten children and records that six sons and three daughters survived her.

William died in 1711. Philippa was left with a young family and the management of his business interests. The monument describes her as “a Young & mournfull Widow”, “Charged with the Care of Ten helpless Infants”. These are the family’s words of remembrance, preserved in stone.

sections.title: Taking charge of the gunpowder mills

paragraphs.text: Philippa took over an enterprise with a London office and production at Balham and Waltham Abbey. Peace in 1713 brought a fall in demand after the War of the Spanish Succession. She closed the Balham operation and concentrated production at Waltham Abbey.

In January 1719 she bought three more powder mills and rights to the Mill Stream. Her son John joined in 1723 with a quarter share, becoming an equal partner in 1730. Philippa continued to take an active part in the business.

Her achievement was in ownership and management: directing an industrial enterprise through difficult trading conditions. It should not be confused with the physical manufacturing work carried out by the people employed at the mills.

Philippa’s son, Philip Walton, became Rector of Mickleham in 1745. Westminster School’s archive identifies him as the son of William and Philippa and records his appointment as 6 February 1744/5, using the contemporary double-year date.

The British Library’s Hardwicke Papers catalogue also identifies Philip as Rector of Mickleham in records dated 1751–1753. Philippa therefore lived during the early years of her son’s ministry here. Her monument records her death on 7 December 1749.
The monument remains a historical object in its own right. Historic England identifies it as an “ashlar and marble rococo wall monument”, with shell features and a swan-neck pediment.

Its inscription is also unusually personal. It honours Philippa’s care for her children: she “secured and improved their Property” and “formed their Minds by her Instructions & Example”. These selected words describe both practical responsibility and the family’s affection for her.

The monument spells her name PHILLIPA. The article uses Philippa, as in the Royal Gunpowder Mills history. It records her death “in the 74th Year of her Age”; we retain that wording rather than treating it as an exact modern statement of age.
The Walton family continued at Waltham Abbey after Philippa’s death. The Crown bought the mills in 1787; the site became the Royal Gunpowder Mills.

Modern recognition has brought her industrial achievements to a wider audience. A blue plaque at the Royal Gunpowder Mills honours her as a “Pioneering industrialist and entrepreneur”. The Essex Women’s Commemoration Project lists her among the women it has commemorated.
At Mickleham, her memorial offers another way into that story: a surviving object, a family’s tribute and a connection between parish life and the history of industry.

timeline: William dies; Philippa takes responsibility for family and business.
Three further mills and Mill Stream rights are acquired.
John joins as a quarter-share partner.
Philippa dies, in the words of her memorial, in her 74th year.

entries.title: Sir Carl Aarvold
entries.description: Rugby international, Recorder of London and Westhumble neighbour. A memorial at St Michael’s opens a story of village service, wit and friendship.

image.alt: Oval stone memorial to Sir Carl Aarvold on the white church wall at St Michael and All Angels

entries.transcription:
Remembered with love and affection
SIR CARL AARVOLD
1907–1991
RECORDER OF LONDON AND SPORTSMAN
A staunch supporter and lifelong friend of this community

“There’s nothing worth the wear of winning
but laughter and the love of friends”.
H. BELLOC

story.standfirst: The Old Bailey knew him as Recorder of London. Westhumble remembered the neighbour who chaired a stormy village meeting and cooked breakfast for friends after a dance.
story.caption: Sir Carl Aarvold’s memorial inside St Michael and All Angels, Mickleham. Photograph supplied for this feature.
story.transcriptionNote: The inscription is set out below in reading order.

paragraphs.text: After a Westhumble Association dinner dance at the Burford Bridge Hotel, Sir Carl Aarvold cooked breakfast sausages for friends at Foxbury. The April 1991 parish obituary remembers that small act of hospitality alongside the warmth he showed to the people who brought the post, delivered the milk, collected the rubbish and tended the garden. Local historian Ronald Shepperd dates Aarvold’s arrival at Foxbury to 1934.

The same tribute recalls a tense Association meeting at the Stepping Stones. A heckler spoke at length in favour of building twenty council houses in the field opposite. Aarvold, who was in the chair, let him finish. His entire reply, as the obituary remembered it, was “InDEED!”

Born in Hartlepool on 7 June 1907, Carl Douglas Aarvold went to Durham School. A school report from March 1925 records that he took over as captain after Christmas. The report follows the chances he made for other players and singles out the pace of his attack. At Emmanuel College, Cambridge, he won four rugby Blues and played in four successive Varsity Match wins. He also won the 220-yard low hurdles at the university’s senior sports meeting in 1927.

He scored eight tries in four internationals on the 1927 tour of Argentina. He made his England debut against Australia at Twickenham and was part of the 1928 Grand Slam side. On the 1930 tour of New Zealand and Australia he captained the British side in eight matches and played in five Tests. His old school recorded in March 1932 that he had captained England throughout the season. He finished with sixteen England caps.

paragraphs.text: During the Second World War Aarvold served with the Royal Artillery in the Territorial Army. The June 1945 Birthday Honours list records him as a temporary lieutenant-colonel and appoints him an Officer of the Order of the British Empire in the military division. The 1968 honours notice also lists his Territorial Decoration, abbreviated T.D.

Aarvold entered the Inner Temple in 1926 and was called to the Bar on 17 November 1932. After the war he joined the North-Eastern Circuit. The Inner Temple records him becoming Common Serjeant of the City of London in 1954, a Bencher of the Inn in 1959 and Recorder of London in 1964. He remained Recorder until 1975. The 1968 New Year Honours list announced his knighthood.

A statutory instrument shows another side of the Recorder’s work. In May 1967 Aarvold made procedural rules for original civil actions in the Mayor’s and City of London Court, with the concurrence of the Rule Committee of the Supreme Court. The rules took effect that July.

In 1973 Aarvold, Sir Denis Hill and G. P. Newton reported on how patients subject to special restrictions were discharged and supervised. They proposed an independent board to advise the Home Secretary on difficult cases involving discharge or transfer from special hospitals. Parliament later confirmed that the board was set up that September.

sections.title: What the records say about the Kray trials

paragraphs.text: The Lions player profile associates Aarvold with a Kray twins trial. The Inner Temple archivists examined the claim about a 1965 case and could find no firm evidence that he presided. Contemporary reporting identifies Mr Justice Melford Stevenson as the judge in the separate 1969 Old Bailey murder trial. Aarvold’s role in the earlier proceedings remains unverified.

A deed dated 26 March 1956 appointed Aarvold a custodial trustee of Mickleham Village Hall. The hall’s history records him as a continuing trustee in 1961, 1968 and 1970, and as retiring in October 1978. The custodial trustees held the hall property in trust.

The parish tribute also remembers him serving on Dorking Urban District Council and the National Trust’s Box Hill Management Committee, and helping campaigns to raise money for the parish church’s restoration. The Box Hill School Trust’s register separately records his directorship, which ended on 17 March 1991.

On 3 September 1981, as president of the Westhumble Association, Aarvold signed the foreword to Ronald Shepperd’s The Manor of Wistomble. The Association published the book the following year. Aarvold thanked Shepperd for showing residents how the places they knew had come to be and hoped he would go on to write about Norbury, Polesden, Fredley and Mickleham.

He ended with a matter of village spelling. Readers could go back to the old name Wistomble, he said, but he had no time for the two-word West Humble. Westhumble, as one word, was the place he was proud to call home.

sections.title: Family and life beyond the bench

paragraphs.text: In July 1934 he married Noeline Hill, the year Shepperd places his arrival at Foxbury. The contemporary school notice and a later genealogy give different days for the wedding. A 1947 notice in the same school magazine records the arrival of their third son.

Years after his last England match, Aarvold was still a familiar figure in sport. Shepperd remembered seeing him at Wimbledon trophy presentations as president of the Lawn Tennis Association. A press photograph from the Getty archive also shows him with association secretary S. B. Reay in a discussion about the Davis Cup.

readMore.title: Aarvold and the Davis Cup
readMore.description: A Getty editorial photograph of Aarvold and S. B. Reay. Rights-managed photograph.
readMore.label: View the Davis Cup photograph at Getty Images

paragraphs.text: The parish tribute remembers Aarvold helping to raise money for the restoration of St Michael’s. The tablet inside the church gives that work a local setting, beside the public roles for which he was known further afield.

Aarvold died on 17 March 1991. At the thanksgiving service on 25 March, his successor as Recorder, Sir James Miskin, gave the address. Aarvold’s sons read from Revelation and from Henry Scott Holland. Afterwards, the tribute recalls, many of the congregation accepted an invitation back to Foxbury.

The oval tablet at St Michael’s calls him “a staunch supporter and lifelong friend of this community”. Its closing lines, attributed on the stone to H. Belloc, place laughter and friendship above winning.
